body.heading: How it works
paragraphs: Each person prepares two short stories: one that really happened and one they made up. They tell both in the same tone, and everyone else votes on which is true. The teller then reveals the answer and, if the true one was doubted, gets to enjoy the moment properly.

Keep stories short — two or three minutes each. A prompt helps younger storytellers: an animal, a journey, a time you got lost, the strangest thing in your pocket. Stories from grandparents' childhoods are gold here, because nobody can check them.

body.heading: Kind rules for guessing
paragraphs: The game is about enjoying the telling, not catching anyone out. Guessing wrong is the fun, so celebrate the storyteller who fooled everyone rather than teasing the people who believed them.
True stories should be the teller's own to share. If a story involves someone else's embarrassing moment, swap it for one of your own — there are always plenty.

body.heading: A jar of prompts
paragraphs: Keep a jar of prompt slips on a shelf so the next story night starts itself. Add new prompts whenever a real event suggests one. Over time the jar becomes a small archive of what your family finds worth telling.
Grandparents and visiting relatives are natural guest tellers. One true story from another generation can keep a family arguing happily for a week.
